title: Medics unaware of violent arrest
article: Two Windsor police officers who struck a man several times while trying to place him under arrest didn't tell paramedics who rushed the dying patient to hospital about the altercation, a coroner's inquest into the death of Bryan Dukic was told Tuesday.

Under cross-examination by Dukic family lawyer Gino Morga, Windsor-Essex EMS paramedic Robin Smallwood said he was told that Dukic ran from police and resisted arrest but not that the 42-year-old had been struck by police officers on April 5, 2006.
"I assumed there was contact made because he was handcuffed," Smallwood said. "I had no information about how rough it was."

Smallwood said knowing about the altercation "would have been useful" as he tried to resuscitate Dukic on the way to the hospital. The paramedic said he assumed Dukic's severe condition was related to drug use or asphyxia because there were no obvious signs of serious trauma.
Smallwood also said the officers told him Dukic was involved in a fight prior to the arrest when he inquired about the bruising on Dukic's face.
He said there was a small amount of fresh blood between Dukic's upper lip and nose.
Smallwood testified that Dukic was unresponsive when he and his partner, along with an EMS student, arrived.

Dukic, who was lying on his side with his hands cuffed behind his back, had blue lips and his face was turning blue, Smallwood said. He had no pulse and appeared to be on his "last efforts of breathing."
Dukic died at Hotel-Dieu Grace Hospital later that day, following the arrest behind a Russell Street apartment building.

Around 6:20 p.m. that day, Windsor police constables Richard Sieberer and John Ryan followed a Dodge Caravan Dukic was driving to a rear lot behind the building and told him he was under arrest because he was a disqualified driver. The inquest was told the officers followed the Dodge Caravan because it was suspected of frequenting a drug house in the area. The vehicle is owned by Dukic's mother, Anna Dukic.

According to a timeline of the incident presented at the inquest, Dukic told the officers he'd just got out of jail and did not want to go back. When each officer grabbed one of Dukic's arms in an effort to handcuff him, he ran into a nearby field. The officers gave chase and apprehended Dukic, who resisted the arrest, flailing his arms and kicking out his legs, striking the officers. Ryan punched Dukic four or five times in the head while Sieberer knee-kicked Dukic in the ribs before handcuffing him.

When the police transport wagon arrived just after 7 p.m., Dukic complained that his ribs were sore and that he had trouble breathing. He had also struck his head when he fell from a kneeling position, in handcuffs.
Dukic was taken to Hotel-Dieu in medical distress and pronounced dead at 9:43 p.m.

An investigation by the province's Special Investigations Unit cleared Sieberer and Ryan of wrongdoing, concluding that they used reasonable force to restrain Dukic. The lawyer representing the officers and Windsor Police Service, Nancy Jammu-Taylor, told reporters Tuesday she was confident the coroner's inquest -- mandatory when a person dies while in custody -- will show that the officers acted responsibly and "did everything they could" under the circumstances.
But the SIU investigation has not dealt with all the details of the case, Morga said.

An autopsy revealed that Dukic died as a result of massive blood hemorrhaging inside his stomach, caused by three tears on his spleen as a result of blunt force trauma. The damage to the spleen was made worse by an existing medical condition that enlarged the organ, testified Dr. Michael Shkrum, the London Health Sciences Centre pathologist who performed Dukic's autopsy.
Dukic's spleen was five to six times larger than normal at the time of death and more susceptible to injury -- a condition related to Dukic's cirrhosis of the liver, Shkrum said.

Dukic's family doctor, Dr. Jairie Ferasol, told the inquest that Dukic had hepatitis C and drank heavily, which contributed to the scarring of his liver. Dukic was also diagnosed with diabetes, Ferasol said.
Toxicology tests showed that Dukic had cocaine, alcohol, anti-anxiety medicine and traces of Tylenol in his system at the time of death. He also had a small bag of cocaine stuffed inside his mouth.
